task_description:
Given a C program and a target compiler, an automated compiler-autotuning technique
searches for an optimization-flag configuration that minimizes the program's runtime while
preserving its output behavior.
candidate_definition: ONE instance = ONE program at ONE commit, identified by {repository URL, commit hash, program_name}, where program_name is the name of the executable the build produces and the shell invokes. The program must be a runnable command-line program (input on argv or stdin, result on stdout, exits by itself), must build cleanly with NO optimization flags and produce a reproducible output on a reference input, and must also build and run under at least one optimizing configuration including -O3 producing the SAME output. Libraries, kernel modules, firmware, code generators, network servers/clients and programs needing a display are not candidates. A repository that builds several programs may yield several instances.
data_source:
A real, public C codebase or program collection where a candidate can be built with a
standard compiler and produces a deterministic, reproducible output on some input --
which repositories to draw from is not pre-assigned: the builder finds and chooses
sources that meet the admissibility criteria below. The unit of instancehood is exact:
ONE instance = ONE program at ONE commit, identified by {repository URL, commit hash,
program}, where program is the name of the executable the build produces and the shell
invokes -- a repository that builds several programs can yield several candidates, together with its recorded reference inputs and reference
compilations. Reference compilations: at least the -O3 build; further optimizing
configurations are welcome; each is recorded with its flags, its output digest and its
runtime. Candidate = one such program that builds cleanly with NO optimization flags and
produces a reproducible reference output on a reference input, and that also builds and
runs under at least one optimizing configuration (including -O3) producing the SAME
output. The program is a RUNNABLE COMMAND-LINE PROGRAM: it builds into an executable, it
is started from a shell with its input given on the command line or on standard input, it
writes its result to standard output, and it exits by itself. A library source file, a kernel module, firmware, a code generator, a
network server or client, and a program that needs a display are NOT candidates, whatever
the repository is. What makes a program a good source here is where its time
goes: the work must be the program's OWN computation on data it holds -- compressing,
hashing, parsing, searching, transforming, solving -- because that is the work a compiler's
optimizer acts on. A program whose time goes to process startup, to waiting on disk or a
network peer, or to a fixed sleep is a poor source however popular it is, and a daemon or a
client whose work happens on someone else's machine is not a source at all.

WHO DOES WHAT. Finding sources and building instances are two jobs, and the first one is
CHEAP ON PURPOSE. Whoever finds sources screens them from what each repository says about
itself: its metadata (language, history, activity), the presence of documented build
instructions or a standard build file, and its own README and documentation describing
what the program does with the data it is given. On that evidence a source is proposed
when the program plausibly spends its time on its own computation over an input it reads
-- compressing, hashing, parsing, searching, transforming, solving -- and is set aside
when the documentation describes a network daemon or client, a GUI, a program whose work
happens elsewhere, or a project whose own instructions do not say how to build it. A
proposed source names the repository, the commit, the program (the executable's name and
how it is invoked), and where the
build instructions were found; it carries NO timings and NO build of its own, because
nothing is compiled or measured at this stage. The screening evidence is quoted, not
summarised: the proposer records the line of the project's own documentation that shows
how it is built, and the sentence of that documentation describing the computation the
program performs on the data it is given, each copied verbatim from a named file in the
repository so that whoever receives the proposal can find it there unchanged. Fetching
the repository to read those files is expected; compiling it is not. Everything else -- cloning, building under
each configuration, generating the reference inputs, timing them, and every criterion
below -- is the builder's work on the proposed source, and a proposed source that turns
out not to satisfy the criteria is a normal and expected loss there, not a failure of the
screening.

admissibility.name: commit_count
admissibility.observe: git rev-list --count HEAD in a full clone

admissibility.name: build_file
admissibility.observe: GET https://api.github.com/repos/{org}/{project}/contents/ -> the root listing; report the FIRST file name in it that, lowercased, is one of the required set (absence of any such file fails the clause)
admissibility.require: one of [makefile, cmakelists.txt, configure.ac, configure, makefile.am]

criteria:
- the program builds with the target compiler using no optimization flags (the default
  build), and that build exits zero. The recorded build recipe honours an exported CFLAGS:
  one recipe builds the default configuration when CFLAGS=-O0 is exported and the
  optimizing configuration when CFLAGS=-O3 is, and whoever re-runs the recipe (the
  harness, at every probe and every check) exports the flags rather than trusting the
  recipe's own defaults -- a project whose build ignores CFLAGS (its makefile hardcodes
  -O2, say) is not a source until its recipe is written to honour them
- a working setup is established FIRST: some reference input, however small or fast, for
  which the default build produces a reproducible output. No timing requirement applies at
  this point -- an instance is not rejected for being quick before it has been given
  larger inputs to work on
- ONLY THEN, the instance generates SEVERAL further reference inputs of increasing COST
  using a script it carries, and ships all of them -- the small one it started from and
  the larger ones. Cost is measured, not assumed: each shipped input records the default
  build's median runtime on it, and inputs are ordered by that runtime (byte size does
  not predict cost -- a 16-byte config file can be the longest-running input). Inputs
  are generated by scaling parameters of the program's own domain (a bigger corpus to
  compress, a longer wordlist to search, a larger image to resize), never downloaded.
  The costliest input must bring the default build's median runtime to at least 1 second
  (median over at least 5 runs), so a difference between compilations is observable
  rather than lost in process startup, and to at most 10 seconds: every later stage
  re-runs this input some thirty times per instance (five repetitions per side per
  control), so an input that takes minutes turns one instance into hours of machine
  time, and an input large enough to leave the page cache makes every repetition
  I/O-bound and hides the very difference the instance exists to show (a 3 GB input
  separated at 1.15x where 100 x 10 MB from cache separated at 2.46x, same program).
  Generate the largest input INSIDE that band, not the largest input possible. A program
  that cannot be pushed into the band by any input the builder can generate is recorded
  with its achieved runtime and the reason -- an explicit recorded exception, never a
  silent pass. The exception field has exactly one spelling for "no exception applies"
  (the literal `none`) so that a reader can tell the two cases apart mechanically, and a
  non-`none` reason must state a fact the harness can contradict from the record: the
  achieved median runtime and why no generated input raises it (a program whose runtime
  is process startup regardless of input says so; a reason that merely restates that the
  floor was met is not an exception). A runtime that DOES lie in the band with a reason
  other than `none`, or one that does not with `none`, is a contradiction, not a pass
- the costliest input must also make the program's OWN computation the thing being timed.
  Runtime alone is not enough: a run can spend a full second reading files or waiting and
  still leave the optimizer nothing to work on. The observable test is the one the
  instance already records -- the default build's median on the costliest input must be at
  least 1.05 times the -O3 build's median there (a 5% separation, the same factor the
  reference compilations are already compared by). Below that the workload has not been
  shown to be sensitive to compiler flags, and an instance built on it cannot rank flag
  configurations. Such a
  measurement is a verdict on the WORKLOAD, not on the program: the same program under a
  different workload often separates cleanly (walking a repository's history is I/O-bound
  and came out at 1.00x, while hashing a 500 MB file with the same binary came out at
  3.2x). So before a program is set aside for being flag-insensitive, at least one further
  workload of a different KIND -- more computation per byte, less I/O, no startup
  dominance -- must have been tried and recorded
- the program also builds under at least one optimizing configuration including -O3, and
  each such build produces output IDENTICAL to the default build's for the same input --
  exactly for non-floating output, or within the stated numeric tolerance for
  floating-point
- each reference compilation records its own runtime ON THE LARGEST INPUT, so a solver has
  a time to beat; ALL repetition timings (at least 5 runs) are recorded as a list together
  with their mean, median and coefficient of variation -- variance is reported as data,
  never used to exclude an instance (the reason is: measurements on a shared machine compete for resources and a variance threshold there measures the machine's load, not the candidate). Only a measurement rendered meaningless by interference --
  order-of-magnitude outliers across repetitions -- is re-measured rather than shipped
- a compilation that crashes, or whose output differs from the default build's, is
  recorded as such rather than silently dropped -- detecting that difference is what the
  instance's oracle is for
- the program must be deterministic on the chosen reference inputs (or made deterministic
  by supplying fixed seeds/inputs): identical output digest across at least 3 consecutive
  runs in the same environment

- the builder verifies each of these itself before delivering, by running the scripts on its
  own machine: the program does its own computation on the input (not startup, not I/O); the
  output is identical across three runs; the two versions print the same output; break.sh
  changes it; the default build's median runtime on the costliest input lies between 1 and 10
  seconds and is at least 1.05 times the -O3 build's median
- done means: the harness ran every script on a blank machine without a crash, and the builder
  has verified the points above itself and written what it verified, with the numbers and the
  reason for anything it accepted against the harness's observations, into instance.json under
  builder_notes. The harness reports what it observed; the builder judges.
spread: at most 3 per repository (repo_url); at most 1 per candidate (repo_url, commit_sha, program_name); at most 5 per org (repo_url)
territory: Search for C repositories with star count between 100 and 133 inclusive.
sibling_territories: Search for C repositories with star count between 134 and 200 inclusive.
Search for C repositories with star count between 201 and 400 inclusive.
Search for C repositories with star count of 401 or more.
